results.authors: McKeith I, O'Brien J, Walker Z, et al. (NICE-DLB study group)
results.summary: Multicenter study (n=326) demonstrated that 123I-FP-CIT SPECT (DaTscan) has 77.7% sensitivity and 90.4% specificity for distinguishing DLB from AD and other dementias. A normal DaTscan makes DLB substantially less likely and, combined with clinical and biomarker data, supports an alternative diagnosis. DaTscan is listed as a supportive biomarker for DLB in diagnostic criteria.
results.title: Sensitivity and specificity of 123I-FP-CIT SPECT in dementia with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer disease

results.authors: McKeith IG, Boeve BF, Dickson DW, et al.
results.summary: Fourth consensus criteria for DLB. Core clinical features: fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and one or more parkinsonism features. Indicative biomarkers include reduced dopamine transporter uptake on SPECT or PET (DaTscan). A normal DaTscan in a patient with soft core features substantially reduces the probability of DLB. Diagnosis requires at least two core features or one core feature with one indicative biomarker.
results.title: Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium

results.authors: Walker Z, Costa DC, Walker RW, et al.
results.journal: Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
results.summary: Prospective study found that a normal DaTscan in clinically uncertain dementia cases (with some Lewy body features) reliably excluded DLB at post-mortem validation and correctly pointed toward AD or other non-DLB dementias. A positive amyloid biomarker with normal DaTscan provides convergent evidence for AD rather than DLB.
results.title: Usefulness of DaTscan in differentiating dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease

output.summary: DaTscan (123I-ioflupane SPECT) measures presynaptic dopamine transporter availability and is a DLB indicative biomarker. In patients with dementia and overlapping AD/DLB features, a normal DaTscan substantially reduces the probability of DLB (specificity ~90%). However, DaTscan does not diagnose AD; it is used to exclude DLB. Definitive AD diagnosis requires positive amyloid biomarkers (CSF or amyloid PET) combined with compatible clinical presentation. Concurrent positive amyloid PET or CSF ATN profile with a normal DaTscan provides convergent support for AD rather than DLB in patients presenting with mixed features.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Gerald Hoffman is a 72-year-old right-handed retired principal who presents to the neurology memory clinic accompanied by his wife, Eleanor, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past 18 months. His wife first noticed the changes approximately 18 months ago when he began forgetting recent conversations and misplacing items with increasing frequency — he would put keys in the refrigerator and forget where he had stored gardening tools he had used the day before. His longtime interest in crossword puzzles, which he previously completed in ink, has become notably more labored, and he now leaves many incomplete. Over the subsequent year his word-finding difficulties worsened: he frequently struggles to retrieve proper names and low-frequency nouns, sometimes describing rather than naming objects. His wife notes he has become repetitive, asking the same question within an hour.

In the past 2-3 months, new symptoms emerged that concern his wife: she has observed several episodes of blank staring lasting 5-10 seconds during which he does not respond, then resumes activity without any memory of the pause. These occur several times per week. He has also twice reported seeing something that was not there — once a small animal in the kitchen, and once a shadow in the examination room today. He has been somewhat more withdrawn and less interested in social activities, which Eleanor attributes to frustration with his memory. He denies feeling depressed. Sleep is adequate with good CPAP adherence; wife has not observed acting-out of dreams or nocturnal vocalizations. He remains independent in basic ADLs including bathing, dressing, and grooming. He stopped driving one month ago at Eleanor's request after he missed a turn on a familiar route and drove in the wrong direction for several minutes.

The family history is notable for an older brother with diagnosed Parkinson's disease, which Eleanor has read about and wonders whether her husband might have something similar. On careful questioning, she confirms that his personality is unchanged, there has been no new urinary urgency or incontinence, and no falls. He has not had obvious tremor at rest.

neurological_exam.additional: On two occasions during the interview, the patient appeared momentarily confused and stared blankly for 5-10 seconds, then resumed conversation without acknowledgment. Wife describes similar episodes at home, occurring several times per week over the past 2 months, which she attributes to him 'zoning out.' No incontinence, falls, or acting out of dreams reported. During history-taking, patient stated he 'saw a shadow move behind the door' in the examination room — when asked, he said he was not sure whether he truly saw something. Wife confirms one prior episode at home approximately 6 weeks ago where he said he saw a small animal in the kitchen; none has been verified.
